🇺🇸🇷🇺 Blumenthal revives "hell sanctions" bill — this time Trump would have no choice

Senator Richard Blumenthal has unveiled an updated version of the Russia sanctions bill he originally drafted with the late Senator Lindsey Graham. The changes matter — a lot.

Secondary tariffs on countries buying Russian energy have been slashed fivefold, from a threatened 500% down to a maximum of 100%. The White House would still pick which countries get hit and at what rate — but here's the catch: it can't pick zero. Full exemption isn't on the table.

The targets: the five biggest buyers of Russian oil, the five biggest buyers of Russian gas, and five countries deemed most active in helping Russia dodge sanctions. Current data points to China, India, Slovakia, Hungary and Azerbaijan on oil, and China, France, Japan, Hungary and Belgium on gas — meaning several US allies and partners would be staring down American tariffs over energy ties with Moscow.

The bigger shift: under this version, Trump would be legally obligated to sanction Putin personally, along with the entire top tier of Russian leadership. That includes the prime minister, defense minister, chief of the General Staff, commanders of the armed services and military districts, and the heads of the Foreign Ministry, Finance Ministry, Energy Ministry, Industry and Trade Ministry, Agriculture Ministry, Federal Security Service, Foreign Intelligence Service, military intelligence, the National Guard and the Federal Protective Service, all within 30 days of signing.

The bill also bans new US investment in Russia, purchases of Russian sovereign debt, and dealings in securities of Russian state companies. It singles out the Yamal LNG and Arctic LNG 2 projects, along with the Bank of Russia, Sberbank, VTB and Gazprombank.

And unwinding any of it wouldn't be Trump's call alone. Sanctions relief would require the president to certify to Congress that Russia has signed a peace agreement accepted by Ukraine and halted hostilities, a ceasefire alone wouldn't cut it, and Congress would retain the power to block the rollback anyway.

Trump has previously signaled he'd only back a bill that left him full discretion on whether to impose or lift sanctions. Blumenthal's text does the opposite: mandatory sanctions, no unilateral exit, congressional veto over relief. Whether Trump touches this version is an open question.
